title: Develop and implement plant manipulation methods

lessons.title: Why and how plants are manipulated
lessons.html:
Steering plant growth

Plant manipulation means deliberately changing how a plant grows, flowers or fruits to improve yield, quality, timing or ease of management. South African fruit, vine, vegetable and ornamental producers rely on it: pruning and training of apples and table grapes, thinning of stone fruit, girdling of citrus and grapes, use of plant growth regulators, and control of flowering in crops such as pineapples or chrysanthemums.

Basic plant physiology behind manipulation

  • Apical dominance: the growing tip produces hormones (auxins) that suppress side buds. Removing the tip (heading or pinching) encourages branching.
  • Source and sink: leaves (sources) produce sugars that move to sinks (fruit, roots, shoots). Reducing competing sinks, for example by thinning fruit, sends more sugar to the remaining fruit.
  • Balance between vegetative and reproductive growth: excessive vigour often means fewer flowers and poorer fruit colour.
  • Plant hormones: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid control growth, flowering, fruit set, ripening and dormancy.
  • Light interception: fruit colour and bud fertility depend on light reaching the inside of the canopy.

Categories of manipulation

MethodExamples
MechanicalPruning, training, pinching, topping, bending, girdling, root pruning
Crop loadHand, chemical or mechanical thinning
ChemicalRegistered plant growth regulators for fruit set, size, ripening, rest breaking
EnvironmentalShade nets, day length control, temperature, water stress (regulated deficit irrigation)
Propagation-basedRootstock choice to control vigour

Choose methods based on clear objectives: what do you want to change, and how will you measure it?

lessons.title: Pruning, training, thinning and girdling
lessons.html:
Mechanical and crop-load methods

Pruning and training

Training builds the tree or vine's framework in the first years; pruning maintains it.

  • Systems: central leader, open vase, trellis and espalier systems in apples and pears; various trellis systems in table and wine grapes; hedgerow systems in high-density citrus and macadamias.
  • Heading cuts stimulate growth near the cut; thinning cuts remove whole shoots and open the canopy with less regrowth.
  • Prune in dormancy for structure and vigour control; summer pruning reduces vigour and improves light to fruit.
  • Use sharp, clean tools; disinfect between trees where diseases spread on tools.

Thinning

Overloaded trees produce small fruit, break branches and may bear poorly the next year (alternate bearing). Thinning at the right stage gives larger fruit and regular bearing.

  • Hand thinning gives precise control but costs labour.
  • Chemical thinning with registered products is fast but depends on weather and stage; follow the label exactly.
  • Set target fruit numbers per tree or per cm² of trunk cross-section based on industry guidelines.

Girdling

Girdling removes a thin ring of bark from the trunk or cane, temporarily blocking sugar flow to roots so more stays above the cut. In table grapes it is used to improve berry size and in citrus to improve fruit set. The width, timing and tool must follow cultivar guidelines; poor girdling can kill or weaken plants. Never girdle stressed or weak plants.

Safety

  • Ladders: three points of contact, set on firm ground.
  • Wear eye protection and gloves when pruning; keep secateurs closed when moving.
  • Chainsaws only by trained operators with full PPE.
  • Girdling knives are very sharp; cut away from the body.

lessons.title: Growth regulators, environmental methods and evaluation
lessons.html:
Chemical and environmental methods

Plant growth regulators (PGRs)

PGRs are registered as agricultural remedies under Act 36 of 1947, so the same rules apply as for pesticides: use only on registered crops, at label rates and timings, with label PPE and pre-harvest intervals. Uses include:

  • Gibberellins to increase berry size or improve fruit set in some crops.
  • Rest-breaking agents in deciduous fruit in areas with insufficient winter chilling, such as parts of the Western Cape in warm winters.
  • Ethylene-releasing products to promote ripening or colour, or ethylene inhibitors to delay ripening in storage.
  • Growth retardants to reduce vigour or control height in ornamentals.

Effects depend strongly on temperature, crop stage and cultivar. Test on a small block first and keep untreated control rows.

Environmental manipulation

  • Shade nets reduce sunburn and hail damage and can change ripening times.
  • Day length control using lights or blackout to time flowering in short-day or long-day crops.
  • Regulated deficit irrigation: controlled water stress at certain stages to reduce vigour without hurting yield.
  • Rootstocks to control vigour, tolerance to soil problems and precocity.

Developing and implementing a plan

  1. Define objectives per block (e.g. increase class 1 size by 10%).
  2. Select methods and timing based on physiology and guidelines.
  3. Train workers with demonstrations and standards.
  4. Supervise quality and record what was done.
  5. Measure results against untreated or previous seasons: yield, size, colour, return bloom, cost per hectare.

Key points

  • Manipulation works through apical dominance, source-sink balance, hormones and light.
  • Heading cuts stimulate growth; thinning cuts open canopies.
  • Thinning improves fruit size and reduces alternate bearing.
  • Growth regulators are registered remedies: follow the label.
  • Set objectives, keep control rows and measure results.

quiz.question: What happens when the growing tip of a shoot is removed?

options.text: Apical dominance is reduced and side branching increases
